\section{System and Threat Model}\label{sec:system}

\subsection{Components}
PromptGuard has three parts (Fig.~\ref{fig:arch}). A Chrome extension watches the prompt box on
chatgpt.com, chat.openai.com, claude.ai and gemini.google.com. When the user has stopped typing for
\pgnum{e2e.config.debounce_ms}~ms, it sends the text in the box to a REST API and draws a badge next to
the box. The API runs one of the detectors of Section~\ref{sec:data} and returns a label, a confidence,
a risk score, the attack patterns that matched and, when no pattern explains a flag, the words that
contributed most to it. A web dashboard issues API keys with a per-key rate limit, shows request logs and
has a playground for manual tests (Fig.~\ref{fig:explain}). The code is open source, and the API and
dashboard can be self-hosted.

The detectors use three labels, SAFE, SUSPICIOUS and MALICIOUS, which the extension shows as Safe,
Review and Danger. We use the first set throughout. Since the training data has no SUSPICIOUS class of
its own (Section~\ref{sec:data}), our headline metric is binary: SAFE against not SAFE.

\subsection{Threat model}
Two different attacks are often both called prompt injection, and a tool in the user's browser helps
against only one of them.

\emph{Jailbreaks.} The user writes the adversarial prompt, to make the model ignore its own rules. The
user is the attacker and controls the browser, so a client-side detector is no security control here:
it can be switched off. Jailbreaks are part of our training and test data and we report how well they
are detected, but we make no protection claim for them.

\emph{Indirect injection.} The adversarial text comes from a third party, in an email, a web page, a
document or a table, and the user pastes it into the chat together with their own request
\cite{greshake2023not}. The user is the victim. The extension sees the pasted text before it reaches the
model and can warn the user. This is the case PromptGuard targets. The attacker controls the pasted
content, including its wording, but not the extension, the API or the user's own request. Content that
the chat service fetches by itself, such as web results, uploaded files or tool outputs, never passes
through the prompt box and is out of scope, as are agents with tool access \cite{willison2025trifecta}.
Section~\ref{sec:eval} tests this case with injections embedded in pasted documents.

\subsection{Privacy}
While it is enabled and configured, the extension sends the prompt-box text, the API key and the chosen
model to the configured endpoint and nowhere else. The API stores a SHA-256 hash of the text, the label,
scores, matched patterns, latency, model and key; the text itself is stored only if this is turned on
for the key, which it is not by default. An unsalted hash of a short or common prompt can be guessed, so
users who need more than this can self-host the API. The extension keeps the API key in local, unsynced
extension storage, asks for host permission only for the hosted API and, when the user saves another
endpoint, for that one origin, and contains no remote code or analytics.

\section{Data and Models}\label{sec:data}

\subsection{Training data}
We train and select models on the neuralchemy prompt-injection dataset \cite{neuralchemy2025} at a
pinned revision and use its official splits: \pgnum{pr.dataset.source_rows.train} training,
\pgnum{pr.dataset.source_rows.validation} validation and \pgnum{pr.dataset.source_rows.test} test rows,
each labelled benign or malicious. To train the SUSPICIOUS class we derive it inside each split, after
splitting: \pgp{0}{meta.build.suspicious_fraction_of_safe}\% of the SAFE rows get an appended manipulation
phrase, and a small set of hand-written suspicious prompts is assigned to exactly one split by a hash of
its text. Leetspeak variants of \pgp{0}{meta.build.evasion_augment_fraction}\% of the MALICIOUS rows and
benign hard negatives are added the same way. Any derived row whose normalized text also occurs in
another split is dropped, and so is any training row that matches an evaluation row; official
evaluation rows are never dropped. The processed splits have \pgnum{pr.dataset.processed.train.rows},
\pgnum{pr.dataset.processed.validation.rows} and \pgnum{pr.dataset.processed.test.rows} rows. Because
SUSPICIOUS is synthetic, every headline number is binary and computed on the
\pgnum{pr.models.classical.runs.0.binary.n_samples} original test rows with their original labels.

\subsection{Detectors}
\emph{Classical.} TF-IDF features of word 1--3-grams and within-word character 2--5-grams feed a
multinomial logistic regression with balanced class weights. Among \pgnum{trn.classical_model.validation.n_keys}
candidates (logistic regression with four regularization strengths on word or word-plus-character
features, a random forest and multinomial naive Bayes), we keep the one with the highest weighted F1 on
the validation split: word-plus-character features with $C=1$ (validation F1
\pgr{4}{trn.classical_model.validation.logreg_word+char_C_1.three_class.f1_weighted}; the runner-up scores
\pgr{4}{trn.classical_model.validation.logreg_word+char_C_10.three_class.f1_weighted}). The fit is
deterministic, so all seeds give the same model.

\emph{Transformers.} We fine-tune DistilBERT (\texttt{distilbert-base-uncased}, ``bert'') and ModernBERT-base
(``guard'') for \pgnum{bert42.hyperparameters.epochs} epochs at learning rate
\pgsci{bert42.hyperparameters.learning_rate} with inputs truncated to \pgnum{bert42.hyperparameters.max_length}
tokens, batch sizes \pgnum{bert42.hyperparameters.batch_size} and \pgnum{guard42.hyperparameters.batch_size},
over \pgnum{pr.models.bert.summary.n_seeds_ok} and \pgnum{pr.models.guard.summary.n_seeds_ok} seeds.

\emph{Risk score.} The API reports $R=\min(100,\max(0,\,b+\min(4m,15)+20(c-0.5)))$, where $b$ is 15, 55
or 85 for SAFE, SUSPICIOUS or MALICIOUS, $m$ is the number of matched patterns and $c$ the model's
confidence (its largest class probability). The patterns explain a result but never change the label.
The API returns the three terms with the score.

\emph{Rule floor and escalation.} Two rules sit on top of the classical model. A chat-template token
(such as \texttt{<|im\_start|>}) or text hidden entirely in tags raises SAFE to SUSPICIOUS. When the guard
model is loaded, a classical SUSPICIOUS verdict with confidence below 0.65 is replaced by the guard
model's verdict. We evaluate both rules in Section~\ref{sec:eval}.
